name: Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga; his departure from the world is taken to begin the Kali yuga (traditionally 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: The tradition regards him as the Lord (Bhagavān) himself born as Vasudeva's son; in the Gītā he speaks as unborn and imperishable, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6), and the Nārāyaṇīya presents him as a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Vasudeva and Devakī, prince of the Vṛṣṇis, Arjuna's charioteer and teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā and the Anugītā. In the Gītā he speaks as the Lord who descends age after age (4.6–8), is the source of all (10.8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (ch. 11); the Nārāyaṇīya names his birth at Mathurā among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.82). In the Anuśāsana he learns the thousand names of Śiva from Upamanyu (13.14–17).
notes: Historicity recorded as 'legendary' in the scholarly sense only; the tradition holds him to be the Lord incarnate.

name: Arjuna (Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The third Pāṇḍava, the archer, whose refusal to fight his kinsmen occasions the Gītā; he declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and takes refuge in him (2.7), receives the divine eye and the vision of the universal form (11.8ff), and after the war asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the teaching (Anugītā 14.16).

name: Sañjaya

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra's charioteer and counsellor, given divine sight by Vyāsa to see and report the battle (6.2); he narrates the Gītā to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and says he heard it 'by the grace of Vyāsa' directly from Kṛṣṇa (18.75).

name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The blind Kuru king, father of Duryodhana; hearer of the Gītā through Sañjaya, of Vidura's counsel (5.33–40), Sanatsujāta's teaching (5.41–45) and Vidura's consolations (11.2–7); he later retires to the forest (Āśramavāsika).

name: Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: Presented as a seer who knows past, present and future, able to grant divine sight and to foresee the war's outcome; identified with the earlier Apāntaratamas (12.337.54).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Parāśara and Satyavatī, in the tradition the arranger of the Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata; grandfather of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas; gives Sañjaya divine sight, teaches his son Śuka (12.224–247), and tells that in a former birth he was Apāntaratamas, the Veda-teacher born of Nārāyaṇa's word, reborn in Vasiṣṭha's line (12.337.38–54). The Gītā names him among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13) and 'among sages I am Vyāsa' (10.37).

name: Vaiśampāyana

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Vyāsa's disciple who recites the Mahābhārata to king Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice; the narrator of the Nārāyaṇīya to Janamejaya.

name: Ugraśravas Sauti

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Lomaharṣaṇa, the bard who retells the Mahābhārata, as heard at Janamejaya's sacrifice, to the sages assembled for Śaunaka's twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest (1.1).

name: Janamejaya
summary: Kuru king, great-grandson of Arjuna, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions open sections such as the discussion of whether puruṣas are many or one (12.338.1).

name: Śaunaka (of Naimiṣa)
summary: Head (kulapati) of the sages of the Naimiṣa forest, at whose twelve-year sacrifice Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata.
notes: A brāhmaṇa Śaunaka also instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at the start of the exile (3.2, the eightfold path of dharma at 3.2.71); the identity of the two is not asserted here.

name: Bhīṣma (Devavrata, Gāṅgeya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Śaṃtanu and Gaṅgā, the Kuru elder who vowed celibacy; granted mastery over the moment of his death, he lies on a bed of arrows waiting for the sun's northern course (6.114.89–98) and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira in Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma (Śāntiparvan) and in the Anuśāsana, including the thousand names of Viṣṇu; at death his self, restrained in all the openings, pierces the crown and rises to heaven (13.154.5).

name: Yudhiṣṭhira (Dharmarāja)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Dharma; answers the Yakṣa (3.297) and Nahuṣa (3.177), defends acting righteously without seeking its fruit against Draupadī (3.32.4), wishes to renounce after the war and is persuaded to rule (12.7–36), receives Bhīṣma's instruction, and at the end refuses to enter heaven without the dog who was devoted to him (17.3).

name: Draupadī (Kṛṣṇā, Pāñcālī)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Wife of the Pāṇḍavas; in the forest she questions divine justice and argues for human effort against Yudhiṣṭhira (3.28–33), and after the war urges him to rule (12.14).

name: Bhīma (Bhīmasena)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Second Pāṇḍava; argues for artha and action against Yudhiṣṭhira's forbearance (3.34; 12.10); instructed by Hanumān on the ages and the duties of the varṇas (3.147–150).

name: Vidura

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: An embodiment of Dharma; his death by yoga, entering Yudhiṣṭhira, is narrated at 15.33.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, born of a śūdra woman; Dharma incarnate through Māṇḍavya's curse (1.100.28). He counsels Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Viduranīti, 5.33–40) and, declaring that as one born of a śūdra womb he will not speak beyond this, calls Sanatsujāta to teach the higher knowledge (5.41.5); consoles him after the war (11.2–7); dies in the forest by entering Yudhiṣṭhira's body limb by limb and breath by breath (15.33.25).

name: Sanatsujāta
summary: An ever-youthful sage (kumāra) summoned by Vidura's thought, who teaches Dhṛtarāṣṭra that heedlessness is death and heedfulness immortality, and describes the brāhmaṇa, silence, the virtues and the shining Brahman seen by yogins (5.41–45).
notes: The tradition counts him among Brahmā's mind-born sons (not checked here).

name: Dharma (the god; Yama Dharmarāja)
summary: The deity Dharma, father of Yudhiṣṭhira; he tests his son as the Yakṣa at the lake (3.297–298) and as the dog on the great departure (17.3); Vidura is his incarnation (1.100.28).

name: Mārkaṇḍeya
summary: The long-lived sage who instructs the Pāṇḍavas in the forest (3.180–221): on karma, the ages and the dissolution — in which he saw the worlds within the body of a divine child on a banyan branch (3.186.81–91) — the devoted wife and the righteous meat-seller.

name: Nahuṣa
summary: Ancient king cursed to be a python; he seizes Bhīma and is freed when Yudhiṣṭhira answers his questions on who is a brāhmaṇa (3.173–178).

name: Hanumān
summary: Son of the Wind, Rāma's devoted servant in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he meets his brother Bhīma and teaches him the ages of the world and the four sciences — the Veda, economics (vārtā) and polity (daṇḍanīti) (3.147–150).

name: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā (dharmavyādha)
summary: A meat-seller who, living by his inherited work, serving his parents and speaking truth, teaches the brāhmaṇa Kauśika dharma, karma and liberation (3.198–206).

name: Kauśika (the brāhmaṇa of the Vyādha Gītā)
summary: A brāhmaṇa ascetic who burns a crane by his angry glance, is rebuked by a devoted housewife and learns dharma from the meat-seller of Mithilā, then returns to serve his parents (3.196–206).

name: Sāvitrī
summary: Princess who chooses the doomed Satyavat, follows Yama when he takes Satyavat's life and wins it back through her words on dharma and the friendship of the good (3.277–283).

name: Yama
summary: Lord of the dead; in the Sāvitrī episode he takes Satyavat's life and, pleased by Sāvitrī's words, returns it (3.281); in the Jāpaka story he appears with Kāla and Mṛtyu (12.192–193).
notes: U05's contribution; Yama as Naciketas's teacher in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad is covered by U03.

name: Gautamī
summary: An aged brāhmaṇī whose son dies of snakebite; she refuses the vengeance a hunter offers, and in the ensuing debate the serpent, Death and Time each disclaim the cause until karma is named (Anuśāsana 13.1).

name: Bhṛgu
summary: Ancient seer who answers Bharadvāja on creation, the elements, the self, the varṇas and the āśramas (12.175–185).

name: Bharadvāja
summary: Seer who questions Bhṛgu in the Mokṣadharma (12.175–185), raising doubts about the existence of a living self in a body made of elements.

name: Vasiṣṭha
summary: Ancient seer, family priest of the Ikṣvākus; in the Mokṣadharma he teaches Karāla Janaka the Sāṃkhya-Yoga doctrine of the 24 principles, the 25th and the 26th (12.291–296); in the Rāmāyaṇa he is Rāma's preceptor.
notes: His teaching in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is covered by U06.

name: Karāla Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who questions Vasiṣṭha on the perishable and imperishable and on the knowledge of plurality and unity (12.291–296).

name: Yājñavalkya
summary: In the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306) Yājñavalkya teaches king Daivarāti Janaka the evolution of the principles, the guṇas, yoga and dissolution, tells how he won the Yajus teaching from the Sun by austerity (12.306.3–22), and relates his answers to the Gandharva Viśvāvasu (12.306.27); he declares that knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (12.306.85).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account); the Upaniṣadic Yājñavalkya is covered by U03.

name: Daivarāti Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā instructed by Yājñavalkya in the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306).
notes: Whether he is the Upaniṣadic Janaka (tch:janaka) is not asserted.

name: Viśvāvasu
summary: A Gandharva, versed in Vedānta, who puts twenty-four questions and a twenty-fifth on reasoning to Yājñavalkya (12.306.27).

name: Pañcaśikha
summary: In the Mokṣadharma, Pañcaśikha 'Kāpileya' (so called because the brāhmaṇī Kapilā nursed him), 'Āsuri's first disciple', comes to Mithilā and so impresses king Janadeva Janaka that he leaves a hundred teachers to follow him (12.211.6–18); he teaches the Sāṃkhya discrimination (12.211–212); Sulabhā refers to Janaka's having learned from him (12.308).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Āsuri
summary: Named in the Mokṣadharma as the teacher of Pañcaśikha in Kapila's line (12.211.10).

name: Kapila
summary: The Mokṣadharma names Kapila, the supreme seer, as the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60); Nārāyaṇa says the Sāṃkhya teachers call him Kapila (12.326.64); 'among the perfected I am the sage Kapila' (BhG 10.26); in a dialogue Kapila tells Syūmaraśmi that he does not censure the Vedas but that the āśramas' duties have one aim (12.260–262).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Janadeva Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā, occupied with the question of what survives death, instructed by Pañcaśikha (12.211–212).

name: Dharmadhvaja Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who claims to be liberated while ruling and is tested by the ascetic Sulabhā (12.308).

name: Sulabhā
summary: A female mendicant (bhikṣukī) practising the dharma of yoga who wanders the earth alone; doubting king Janaka's liberation, she enters his mind by yoga ('sattva by sattva', 12.308.16) and answers his rebuke with a discourse showing that his attachments remain (12.308).

name: Śuka
summary: Son of Vyāsa, instructed by his father (12.224–247) and by Janaka at Mithilā (12.312–313); he rises by yoga from the peak of Kailāsa into the sky and attains the highest state, while Vyāsa grieves after him (12.318–320).
notes: U05's contribution; his role as reciter of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is covered by U07. The Janaka who teaches Śuka is referenced by the registry id tch:janaka without asserting identity with the Upaniṣadic king.

name: Nārada
summary: Divine seer; in the Nārāyaṇīya he visits Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī and the White Island, where Nārāyaṇa shows himself and teaches him (12.321–339); he asks Asita Devala about the origin of beings (12.267) and relates the origin of Death (12.248–250); he tells Vālmīki the story of Rāma (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1). 'Among divine seers I am Nārada' (BhG 10.26).
notes: U05's contribution; the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is covered by U25.

name: Asita Devala
summary: Sage named in the Gītā among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13); he teaches Nārada the five eternal elements with time as the sixth (12.267.1–6), and learns equanimity from the yogin Jaigīṣavya (12.222; 9.49).

name: Jaigīṣavya
summary: A yogin mendicant who, unmoved by praise or blame, teaches Asita Devala equanimity (12.222) and, at a tīrtha on the Sarasvatī, shows Devala his yogic powers, moving unseen between the worlds (9.49).
notes: The Yoga-bhāṣya's mention of Jaigīṣavya is covered by U10.

name: Tulādhāra
summary: A merchant of Vārāṇasī who teaches the ascetic Jājali that the eternal dharma is friendliness and non-injury to all beings (12.253–256).

name: Jājali
summary: A proud ascetic, on whose head birds nested while he stood motionless, sent to learn dharma from the merchant Tulādhāra (12.253–256).

name: Syūmaraśmi
summary: A sage who, entering a sacrificial cow, challenges Kapila's exclamation at the Vedas (12.260–262).

name: Maṅki
summary: A man who, after losing his young bulls, renounces desire and speaks the Maṅki Gītā (12.171).

name: Piṅgalā
summary: A courtesan who, waiting in vain for a lover, gave up hope and slept happily; her saying 'freedom from hope is the highest happiness' is quoted in the Mokṣadharma (12.168.52).

name: Senajit
summary: A king grieving for his son, consoled by a brāhmaṇa who cites Piṅgalā (12.168).

name: Medhāvin
summary: The son in the father–son dialogue of the Mokṣadharma (12.169), who urges his father to seek the self now because death is always near.

name: Prahlāda
summary: Daitya king; in the Mokṣadharma he explains to Indra that all states arise and cease by their own nature (svabhāva), so pride and grief are baseless (12.215), and questions a sage living like a python (12.172).

name: Bali Vairocana
summary: The defeated Daitya king who tells Indra that Time takes and gives all, and bears his fall without grief (12.216–218).

name: Vṛtra
summary: The defeated asura whose equanimity is praised and who is taught by Sanatkumāra about Viṣṇu and the six colours of beings (12.270–271).

name: Uśanas (Śukra)
summary: Preceptor of the asuras, who questions Vṛtra (12.270); 'among poets I am Uśanas' (BhG 10.37).

name: Sanatkumāra
summary: Mind-born sage who, in the Vṛtra Gītā, teaches the greatness of Viṣṇu and the six colours of living beings (12.271).
notes: U05's contribution; his teaching in Chāndogya 7 is covered by U03.

name: Parāśara
summary: Seer, father of Vyāsa; he instructs king Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (12.279–287).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Vicakhnu
summary: A king who, pitying the animals at a sacrifice, proclaims non-violence as the highest dharma (12.257).

name: Alarka
summary: A royal sage who first sought to conquer the mind and senses with arrows and then learned that they are conquered only by yoga (Anugītā 14.30).

name: Nārāyaṇa
summary: In the Nārāyaṇīya the supreme Lord, also present as the ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa who with Nara performs austerity at Badarī (both born in Dharma's house, 12.332.19); he shows himself to Nārada in the White Island and teaches the fourfold form, his manifestations and the ekāntin dharma (12.321–339).

name: Uparicara Vasu
summary: A king devoted to Nārāyaṇa who performed a horse sacrifice without slaughter; when he sided with the gods that 'aja' in the injunction means a goat, he fell, and was restored by his devotion (12.322–324).

name: Bṛhaspati
summary: Preceptor of the gods; he officiates at Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323) and questions Prajāpati Manu on the highest knowledge (12.194).

name: Apāntaratamas
summary: Born of Nārāyaṇa's word, the teacher of the Vedas (vedācārya), called by some Prācīnagarbha; Vyāsa says he himself was Apāntaratamas in a former birth (12.337.38–61).

name: Hiraṇyagarbha
summary: Named in the Nārāyaṇīya as the knower (vettā) of Yoga, 'none more ancient' (12.337.60).
notes: U05's contribution; Hiraṇyagarbha as the tradition's founder of Yoga is also treated by U10.

name: Śiva (Maheśvara)
summary: In the epic, Śiva teaches Umā dharma (13.126–134), is named as the proclaimer of the Pāśupata knowledge (12.337.62), grants Arjuna the Pāśupata weapon after testing him as a hunter (3.38–41), and is praised with a thousand names (13.14–17); 'among the Rudras I am Śaṃkara' (BhG 10.23); Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Umā (Pārvatī)
summary: Śiva's consort, who questions him on dharma and herself expounds the dharma of women in the Anuśāsana (13.126–134).

name: Upamanyu
summary: A sage devoted to Śiva who teaches Kṛṣṇa the thousand names of Śiva first revealed by Taṇḍi (13.14–17).

name: Vivasvat (the Sun)
summary: The first recipient of the imperishable yoga from Kṛṣṇa, who passed it to Manu (BhG 4.1).

name: Manu Vaivasvata
summary: Son of Vivasvat, who received the yoga from him and passed it to Ikṣvāku (BhG 4.1).
notes: Distinguished from Svāyambhuva Manu, to whom the Manusmṛti is ascribed.

name: Ikṣvāku
summary: First king of the solar dynasty, who received the yoga from Manu; thus the royal sages knew it until it was lost (BhG 4.1–2).

name: Vālmīki
summary: The first poet (ādikavi), author of the Rāmāyaṇa; told Rāma's story by Nārada (1.1), he utters the first śloka in grief at a hunter's killing of a krauñca bird (1.2.15–18) and teaches the poem to Kuśa and Lava.

name: Rāma (Dāśarathi)
summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, hero of the Rāmāyaṇa, called 'dharma embodied' (3.37.13); he goes into exile to keep his father's word, teaches Bharata on impermanence (2.105) and kingship (2.100), answers Jābāli that truth is the root of all (2.109), and vows protection to whoever seeks refuge (6.18.33); the Nārāyaṇīya names him among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.78).

name: Sītā
summary: Daughter of Janaka of Mithilā and Rāma's wife; the Rāmāyaṇa's exemplar of the devoted wife, taught by Anasūyā (2.117–119).

name: Bharata (Rāma's brother)
summary: Rāma's brother, who refuses the throne and rules as Rāma's regent; Rāma's teachings on impermanence and kingship are addressed to him (2.100–105).
notes: Disambiguated from Bharata Muni (tch:bharata-muni).

name: Vibhīṣaṇa
summary: Rāvaṇa's brother who leaves him and takes refuge with Rāma; Rāma accepts him with the vow to protect all who seek refuge (6.18.33).

name: Jābāli
summary: A brāhmaṇa counsellor who urges Rāma, with arguments that deny the other world, to return and rule; Rāma rejects this, and Vasiṣṭha says Jābāli spoke only to bring Rāma back (Rāmāyaṇa 2.108–110).
notes: Distinct from Satyakāma Jābāla (tch:satyakama-jabala).

name: Viśvāmitra
summary: Royal sage who takes the young Rāma to protect his sacrifice and teaches him (Bālakāṇḍa); in the Āpaddharma, during a famine, he takes a dog's haunch from an outcaste, arguing the case for survival (12.139).

name: Agastya
summary: In the Rāmāyaṇa the sage Agastya teaches Rāma the Āditya Hṛdaya before the final battle (Yuddhakāṇḍa 105/107).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Śabarī
summary: An aged female ascetic (śramaṇī) of the Śabara people who served the sages of Mataṅga's hermitage, receives Rāma and ascends to the heavenly worlds (Rāmāyaṇa 3.73–74).

name: Anasūyā
summary: Ascetic wife of the sage Atri, honoured for her austerities, who teaches Sītā the dharma of the devoted wife (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).

name: Śaṅkara
summary: Author of the oldest extant Gītā commentary, which reads the Gītā as teaching liberation by knowledge of the self with renunciation, action serving to purify the mind; also credited with commentaries on the Sanatsujātīya and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.
notes: U05's contribution only (Gītā and epic works).

name: Rāmānuja
summary: Author of a Gītā commentary reading it as teaching bhakti-yoga to Nārāyaṇa, supported by karma- and jñāna-yoga.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Madhva
summary: Author of a Gītā commentary and the Gītātātparyanirṇaya, and of the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya, reading the epic as proclaiming Viṣṇu's supremacy.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: Author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Author of the Jñāneśvarī, the Marathi verse commentary on the Gītā (1290).
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā, dividing it into three six-chapter sections on action, devotion and knowledge.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Śrīdhara Svāmin
summary: Advaita commentator who emphasizes devotion; author of the Subodhinī on the Gītā (and of the Bhāvārthadīpikā on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa).

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara
summary: Maharashtrian scholar at Vārāṇasī, author of the Bhāratabhāvadīpa, the commentary on the whole Mahābhārata that fixed the vulgate text.

name: Keśava Kāśmīrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nimbārka-school teacher credited with a Gītā commentary (Tattvaprakāśikā).

name: Yāmuna
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha summarizing the Gītā in 32 verses.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Vedānta Deśika
summary: Author of the Tātparyacandrikā on Rāmānuja's Gītābhāṣya.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jayatīrtha
summary: Author of the Prameyadīpikā and Nyāyadīpikā on Madhva's Gītā works.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Bhāskara
summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin credited with a Gītā commentary defending the combination of knowledge and works.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin
summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Sārārthavarṣiṇī on the Gītā.

name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Gītābhūṣaṇa (and the Govinda-bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra).

name: Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna)
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on many of Śaṅkara's works, including the Gītābhāṣya.

name: Dhanapati Sūri
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya.

name: Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri author credited with the Sarvatobhadra commentary on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.
notes: Not identified here with the Saiddhāntika Rāmakaṇṭha (tch:ramakantha).

name: Devabodha
summary: Early commentator on the Mahābhārata (Jñānadīpikā).

name: Parāśara Bhaṭṭar
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, son of Kūrattāḻvāṉ, author of the Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa on the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

name: Govindarāja
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava commentator on the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (the Bhūṣaṇa).

name: Bāl Gaṅgādhar Tilak
summary: Scholar and political leader whose Gītā Rahasya (1915) argues that the Gītā teaches action (karma-yoga) by the enlightened rather than renunciation.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
summary: Leader who called the Gītā his 'mother' and read it as teaching action without attachment to fruits (anāsakti) and non-violence; author of Anāsakti Yoga.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Sri Aurobindo
summary: Author of the Essays on the Gita (1916–20).
notes: U05's contribution only; his lineage is owned by U52.

name: Vallabha
summary: Founder of the Puṣṭimārga; counts the Gītā among the four authorities and expounds its meaning in the first section of his Tattvārthadīpanibandha.
notes: U05's contribution only.
